title: Half-Life: On Your Own
subject: physical science
instructions: Answer on your own, even though you did the lab with your group. Write your ID number, not your name.

questions.skill: I can use half-lives to predict what's left
questions.prompt: Halving: A sample starts with 800 atoms, and its half-life is 2 hours. Fill in how many atoms are left.
questions.notes: Each 2 hours, half are left. A student who subtracts 400 each time gets 400, 0: that's a straight line, not halving.

questions.skill: I can use half-lives to predict what's left
questions.prompt: How Old? Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years. A bone has 1/4 of the carbon-14 it had when the animal died. How old is the bone?
questions.key: 1/4 left is two half-lives (1 → 1/2 → 1/4), so 2 × 5,730 = 11,460 years. Look for 5,730 × 4 = 22,920 (counting quarters as four half-lives) or 5,730 ÷ 4.
questions.notes: Newer measurements put carbon-14's half-life at 5,700 years, so 11,400 is also right if the student says so.

questions.skill: I can explain radioactive decay as chance
questions.prompt: Lucky Atom: In your lab, one atom stayed printed side up for five spills in a row. What is true about the next spill?

options.text: It is due to decay, so it will almost surely land blank side up.
options.why: Each spill is a fresh chance; the atom has no memory.

options.text: It still has about a one-half chance of decaying.
options.why: Yes: every spill is the same chance for every atom left.

options.text: It will never decay, because it is a stable atom.
options.why: Every atom in the cup can land blank side up.

options.text: It will decay only after all the other atoms do.
options.why: Atoms don't take turns; each spill is chance.

questions.skill: I can explain radioactive decay as chance
questions.prompt: Smooth or Bumpy? Your group's counts didn't halve exactly each spill, but a real sample with trillions of atoms halves almost exactly. Explain why.

rubric.criterion: Chance: says each atom decays (or lands) at random, so the number that decays each spill varies.
Few atoms: says with few atoms, chance makes big differences from half (e.g., 7 atoms can't split in half; 3 of 5 is far from half).
Many atoms: says with huge numbers, the ups and downs average out, so the fraction is very close to half.
